stem: Earth's outermost solid layer is the
explanation: The crust is the thin outer shell. Beneath it lies the mantle, then the outer core and the inner core.

stem: The thickest of Earth's main layers by volume is the
explanation: The mantle extends from the base of the crust to the outer core and makes up most of Earth's volume. The crust is thin by comparison.
The inner core is solid metal, mostly iron with some nickel. The outer core is the liquid metal layer around it.

stem: Oceanic crust is, compared with continental crust,
explanation: Oceanic crust is basaltic, thin, and dense. Continental crust is thicker, lighter, and often granitic.

stem: Granite is a typical rock of the
explanation: Continents contain large amounts of granite and similar light-coloured rocks. The ocean floor is mainly basalt.

stem: Basalt is a common rock of the
explanation: Basalt is a dark, fine-grained igneous rock that forms the ocean floor and many lava flows.

a: the squeezing of limestone with no melting or change
explanation: Magma or lava cools and crystallises to make igneous rock. Granite and basalt are examples.

b: the accumulation and hardening of sediment
c: the direct cooling of magma in every case
explanation: Sand, mud, and the remains of organisms settle and become rock. Sandstone, shale, and limestone are sedimentary.

stem: Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are
a: changed by heat and pressure without complete melting
b: melted and then cooled as lava at the surface
explanation: Metamorphism alters a rock in the solid state. Marble from limestone, and slate from shale, are examples.

stem: Marble is the metamorphic form of
explanation: Heat and pressure recrystallise limestone into marble. Slate, by contrast, comes from shale.

a: fresh lava that has just cooled
explanation: Organisms are buried in sediment. The heat of magma would destroy them, so fossils are rare in igneous and many metamorphic rocks.

b: a naturally occurring inorganic solid with a definite composition and crystal structure
explanation: Quartz is a mineral. Granite is a rock made of several minerals, including quartz and feldspar.

a: a solid mixture of one or more minerals
b: always a single crystal of one element
explanation: Rocks are aggregates. A piece of granite contains several minerals locked together.

stem: The hardest mineral on the Mohs scale is
explanation: Diamond is 10, the top of the Mohs scale. Talc is 1, the softest standard mineral.

stem: Talc is used as the soft end of the Mohs scale and has hardness
explanation: Talc can be scratched by a fingernail. Diamond, at 10, scratches every other mineral.

stem: Quartz has a Mohs hardness of
explanation: Quartz is harder than steel and than feldspar, and it sits at 7. It is a very common mineral.

a: the breakdown of rock in place
b: the transport of sediment by a river
explanation: Weathering loosens and decomposes rock where it stands. Erosion is the removal and carrying away of the pieces.

a: the breakdown of rock with no movement
b: the growth of a crystal in place
d: the removal and transport of weathered material
explanation: Rivers, wind, ice, and waves carry sediment away. That transport is erosion, which follows weathering.

d: dissolving the whole mountain in one day
explanation: Ice freezes onto rock and pulls pieces away, which is plucking. Rock frozen in the ice also scrapes the bed, which is abrasion.

stem: The theory of plate tectonics says that the outer Earth is
c: one unbroken shell that has never moved
explanation: The lithosphere is broken into plates. They separate, collide, or slide past one another.
Divergence opens a gap that magma fills. Mid-ocean ridges are the common example.
Convergence leads to collision or to one plate sinking under the other. Mountains, trenches, and earthquakes result.

stem: Continental drift, as proposed by Wegener, argued that
a: the oceans are older than the Earth
c: the continents were once joined and have since moved
explanation: Wegener pointed to matching coasts, fossils, and rocks. Plate tectonics later explained how the movement happens.

stem: Pangaea is the name given to
explanation: The continents were assembled in one large land mass, Pangaea, before they separated. The matching shapes of South America and Africa are a familiar clue.

a: the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle
explanation: Tectonic plates are pieces of lithosphere. Below them, the asthenosphere is hotter and can flow slowly.

stem: Magma is molten rock that is
explanation: Molten rock underground is magma. Once it reaches the surface it is called lava.

c: molten rock that has reached the surface
explanation: Lava is magma that has erupted. It cools to form volcanic igneous rock such as basalt.

d: only in the ocean as sediment
explanation: Slow cooling underground allows large crystals, as in granite. Fast cooling at the surface gives fine grains, as in basalt.

stem: Large crystals in an igneous rock suggest that it cooled
b: in a few seconds at the surface
c: as a sediment in a river
explanation: Crystals need time to grow. A coarse rock such as granite cooled slowly, usually deep underground.

d: a sedimentary rock made of sand grains
explanation: Sand is deposited, buried, and cemented into sandstone. The grains are often quartz.

c: the shells and skeletons of marine organisms
explanation: Many limestones are made of calcium carbonate from marine life. They are sedimentary rocks.
Mudstone or shale, squeezed and heated, becomes slate, which splits into sheets. Marble comes from limestone, not from shale.

a: the ways rocks change from one type to another
d: a fixed set of rocks that never change
explanation: Igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks can be weathered, melted, or altered into one another. That continuous change is the rock cycle.

stem: A volcano is an opening where
b: sedimentary rock is deposited by a river
explanation: Magma rises and erupts as lava, ash, or gas. The build-up of that material forms the volcanic cone.

d: at random in the middle of every continent
explanation: Magma is generated where plates separate or where one plate sinks. The Pacific Ring of Fire is the clearest belt.

b: the dissolving or alteration of minerals by water and air
c: the splitting of rock by ice with no chemical change
explanation: Rainwater can dissolve limestone, and oxygen can rust iron minerals. Breaking rock by frost, without a chemical change, is mechanical weathering.

stem: Frost shattering is a form of
explanation: Water freezes in cracks, expands, and pries the rock apart. The pieces are unchanged in composition, so the weathering is mechanical.

a: the cooling of the inner core
c: the deposition of pure salt in every climate
d: weathering of rock together with organic matter
explanation: Broken and chemically altered rock mixes with humus from plants and animals. Climate, slope, and time control the soil that results.

stem: A sedimentary layer is called a
explanation: Sediments are laid down in layers. A single layer is a bed, or stratum, and several are strata.

stem: In an undisturbed sequence, the youngest sedimentary layer is
explanation: New sediment is laid on top of older sediment. Unless the pile is overturned, the top bed is the youngest.

a: a gap in the rock record
b: a perfect continuous sequence with no missing time
explanation: If erosion or non-deposition interrupts the sequence, the contact between older and younger rocks is an unconformity. Time is missing from the record.

stem: Folding of rocks is evidence of
explanation: Layers bend into anticlines and synclines when they are squeezed while warm or deeply buried. Brittle rock may fault instead.

stem: An anticline is a fold in which the layers
explanation: An anticline is an upfold, with the oldest beds near the centre. A downfold is a syncline.

stem: A syncline is a fold in which the layers
d: stand as a vertical dike of magma
explanation: A syncline is a downfold. Younger beds lie toward its centre if the fold has not been overturned.

a: occupies pores and cracks below the surface
c: is the water vapour in a cloud
explanation: After rain soaks in, water fills the spaces in soil and rock. That subsurface water is groundwater.

a: a layer that lets no water through
d: a body of rock or sediment that can yield water
explanation: Porous and permeable material such as sand or sandstone can store and transmit groundwater. A layer that blocks water is an aquiclude.

c: the ability of a material to let fluid pass through
explanation: A permeable rock has connected pores or cracks. Clay may hold water but pass it very slowly, so its permeability is low.

stem: The Himalayas are geologically young mountains formed by
b: the collision of India with Eurasia
c: the spreading of a mid-ocean ridge in Sindh
d: the cooling of the inner core
explanation: The Indian plate is still pushing northward. The collision thickens the crust and lifts the Himalayas.

d: a metamorphic rock formed at depth
explanation: Rivers drop sand, silt, and clay on floodplains and in deltas. That river deposit is alluvium, and much of the Indus plain is covered by it.

d: a river drops sediment as it enters a standing body of water
explanation: The flow slows at the mouth, so the river cannot carry its load. The Indus has built a delta where it meets the Arabian Sea.
